report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false.** The strongest direct evidence is a large randomized trial (1,147 cesarean patients) comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol with iodine–alcohol. Surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in 4.0% versus 7.3%, respectively (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90; *P*=0.02)—an absolute reduction of 3.3 percentage points (about 1 fewer infection per 30 preparations).  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

The result is not completely uniform across every study. CAPICA, a pragmatic randomized trial, found no statistically significant SSI reduction with chlorhexidine–alcohol compared with an *aqueous* povidone-iodine scrub-and-paint regimen (reported rates about 6.3% and 7.0%). That is relevant uncertainty, but it is not the same comparator as iodine–alcohol.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/

Evidence syntheses support a modest benefit: the Cochrane review judged chlorhexidine probably slightly more effective than povidone-iodine for preventing post-cesarean SSI, with moderate-certainty evidence.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section

The key qualification is specificity: evidence does **not** establish that chlorhexidine is superior to every iodine formulation in every setting; trial formulations, application methods, and populations differ, and direct RCT comparisons remain limited. But for the statement as written—chlorhexidine–alcohol versus iodine–alcohol before cesarean—the best direct trial demonstrates a statistically significant reduction, so rejecting it as false is not justified.
